data.title: It's almost impossible to sell a condo unit -2-
data.description:
Over the last five years, condominium units in Louisiana saw the biggest drop in median list prices. Between 2021 and 2026, condo-unit prices in the state were down nearly 17%, Realtor.com data revealed.

Condo units in Washington, D.C., and Colorado followed. In D.C., condo-unit listing prices were down nearly 11% over the last five years; in Colorado, they were down nearly 10%.

Below are the states, plus D.C., where the prices of condominium units have fallen the most over the last five years:

How to avoid buying a 'real-estate lemon'

Some house hunters might consider buying a condo unit as an entry point to homeownership. Experts offered one key piece of advice for those looking to do so: Do extensive research before committing.

Prospective buyers should examine information such as financial-reserve studies, to see if the condo association can cover unexpected costs or emergencies; the milestone report certification - an evaluation by a licensed engineer or architect that confirms the building's structural safety and whether it's up to state and local codes; and the building's insurance policy, according to Andrew Lester, president of FirstService Financial, a residential property-management company that works with thousands of HOAs and condo associations.

"The property manager has got to know the age of the roof, the plumbing, the elevator. Ask for information surrounding the condo," Lester told MarketWatch. The real-estate agent should have the information, too, or be willing to find out, he said.

"Anything that's missing, or any delay in answers - that's a red flag," Lester added. Go to other buildings, get the same information and compare them, he said.

In Virginia, buyers should expect the condo association to provide potential buyers with a booklet disclosing any pending lawsuits, any planned big repairs and the amount of financial reserves they have, Colgan said.

Read the document closely yourself, Lester said. You can also try uploading it into an artificial-intelligence platform such as ChatGPT - which can make errors, so proceed with caution - and ask questions about the potential for a surge in HOA fees and about home-price trends in the area, he added. Then, ask your real-estate agent the same questions.

'I feel trapped' with my condo unit, owner says

Will Hudson is still weighing his options. If he sold the Colorado condo unit right now, he could lose the $58,000 he put down, and possibly more, factoring in broker fees and closing costs.

Losing such a large amount "would absolutely ruin me financially," he said. "I feel trapped."

-Aarthi Swaminathan

data.title: It's almost impossible to sell a condo unit these days: 'I feel trapped'
data.description:
By Aarthi Swaminathan

The condominium market is buckling, real-estate experts say

In some markets, sellers of units in condominiums are more likely to cut prices than sellers of single-family homes, one economist said.

When Will Hudson bought his condominium unit in Golden, Colo., two years ago, the last thing he expected was to be trapped with the real-estate equivalent of a lemon.

With fond memories of living in the condominium complex in his 20s, the 43-year-old public employee decided to buy a two-bedroom unit, sight unseen, for $260,000 in July 2024. At the time, he was living with his fiancée in Bordentown, N.J., and wanted to give Colorado a try.

That purchase quickly turned out to be "the greatest mistake of my life," Hudson told MarketWatch. Within a year of moving in, he wanted to sell, because multiple issues - from water shutoffs to flooding in common areas - made living there difficult.

But a similar property in the complex was already on the market and wasn't selling, prompting him to hold off on listing his. After cutting the asking price from $270,000 in May 2025 to $149,000 in mid-September 2026, the other owner is finally under contract, but the sale has yet to close. Hudson is watching that listing closely while he decides whether to put his unit on the market.

Hudson said he wants to sell in part because he's fed up. His homeowners-association fees have been creeping up to nearly $470 per month, and that's on top of expenses stemming from special assessments he's had to cough up. Living conditions haven't been great; over one recent weekend, his unit had no water or sewer service for two days.

Hudson's frustration mirrors the plight of many owners of condominium units across America.

As home-insurance premiums hit new highs, condo-unit owners are seeing surging HOA fees as their buildings' rising insurance costs are passed on to residents. Special assessments, one-time fees that owners pay to fund shared expenses, are also on the rise. They're more commonly levied on older buildings and communities with shrinking financial reserves, according to Vantaca, an HOA-management platform that works with property-management companies.

For instance, 8.5% of buildings constructed before 2000 had a special assessment in 2025, with the typical owner footing a bill of nearly $2,500 per unit. Across all buildings, the median special assessment bill has risen from $930 to $1,100 in the last four years.

And monthly assessments and other fees are poised to go up even more. More than half of community associations (54%) plan to increase their fees to cover expenses like insurance costs and to help meet new standards for financial reserves that go into effect in 2027.

Even if a unit in a condominium comes with a lower price tag, relative to a detached property, selling one has become more difficult as buyers get spooked at the prospect of bearing ever-rising costs. At a time when home sellers across the country are struggling, owners of condo units have it particularly bad.

"It used to be that a condo would allow you to enter the market because they typically were at a lower price point, and were easier to qualify for," said Ashley Harris, director of home-buyer education at Neighbors Bank, a mortgage lender. But now, with surging HOA fees, "a condo might be more expensive per month" than a single-family home, she said.

In August, condo and co-op sales were down 2.7% compared with the same month last year, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Weakening demand has led to more condominium units on the market. For example, in the area from New Jersey to Virginia served by the multiple-listing service Bright MLS, condo units now account for 15% of active inventory - up from less than 10% prior to the pandemic, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant told MarketWatch.

"In our market, condo sellers are having to make price adjustments more often than single-family-home sellers," Sturtevant said.

HOA fees are rising fast

In 2025 the median HOA fee nationally was $135, up from $108 in 2019. In Florida, they've gone up even more; in the Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach metro area, a median-priced $425,000 home came with a $617-per-month HOA fee, up from $401 in 2019, according to a report by Realtor.com.

And it's getting increasingly hard to find a house that's not in an HOA. In 2025, 44% of homes for sale in the U.S. required owners to pay HOA fees, up from 34% in 2019, Realtor.com found.

To be clear, HOA fees are not exclusive to condominiums. Townhouse and single-family-home owners also pay HOA fees if the property is part of a homeowners association. About a third of single-family homes have HOAs, Realtor.com found - but the share is significantly smaller than the 85% of condo units and townhouses that fall under the jurisdiction of an HOA.

(Realtor.com is operated by News Corp subsidiary Move Inc.; MarketWatch publisher Dow Jones is also a subsidiary of News Corp.)

Related: HOA fees are becoming more common for single-family homes - and top $500 a month in these hot spots

Insurance is a big factor behind the HOA-fee increases for condo-unit owners. While some insurers are charging higher premiums, others are dropping condo HOAs and their owners altogether due to rising losses from natural disasters, such as hurricanes and wildfires, and increasing reinsurance costs. The rising cost of repairing damage, particularly in older buildings, is also driving some insurers to drop or limit coverage.

Some states are stepping in to address the issue. In 2025, following multiple complaints that condominium buildings' master policies were either being canceled or not renewed, Missouri's Department of Commerce and Insurance told insurers to avoid doing so.

A condominium losing its master policy can have severe consequences for owners of units, sellers and even potential buyers, because it leaves the entire building uninsured. That means that if the building's elevator collapses or there is a fire that severely damages the building, homeowners are on the hook for the repairs. The people who own units in the building potentially face large out-of-pocket costs.

Chris Colgan, a Virginia-based real-estate agent with the Real Brokerage, told MarketWatch that a client whom he helped buy a home a few years ago called him up recently and asked if a special assessment levied on owners of units in the condominium, coupled with an increase in monthly fees, was legal. It was.

"He wants to move soon, in the next couple of months, and he was worried about the [rising fees] hurting his resale value," Colgan said. The reason for the increase in fees and the special assessment of around $2,500 was that the association needed more money to keep its insurance policy.

"At some point, some of these condo-association dues are [becoming] more than a car payment," Colgan noted, even as some older buildings don't have sufficient amenities to justify the higher fees stemming chiefly from insurance costs.

Condo units without the right insurance become unsellable

Lack of insurance also affects mortgage financing - and whether prospective buyers can get a loan.

When a buyer wants to purchase a home with a conventional mortgage, that loan is generally backed by Fannie Mae (FNMA) or Freddie Mac (FMCC). The two government-sponsored enterprises require condo associations to maintain a master insurance policy that covers 100% of the units' replacement-cost value estimate, among other standards.

When buildings can't pay for or lose the master policy, it makes it tough to sell a unit because prospective buyers wouldn't be able to qualify for a traditional mortgage.

Changes at the federal level are poised to make purchases in condominiums even more complicated. In March of this year, Fannie and Freddie announced new, stricter financing standards that will require more scrutiny of a condo building's finances.

The upshot is that it's harder for buyers to get mortgages, and the new lending standards are "affecting demand for condo units across the country, especially in the places where insurance issues are more pronounced," Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com, told MarketWatch. "It's already hurting resale values."

In Colorado, Hudson is facing an insurance issue. When he was buying his unit, the lender he initially approached had been unwilling to give him the loan because the HOA's master insurance policy covering the roof was inadequate and didn't meet federal guidelines. At his real-estate agent's urging, he found an alternative lender, but he had to put down 20%.

Now he might not be able to find a buyer when and if he puts the unit up for sale, Hudson said, because a buyer might not be able to get a mortgage for the same reason that initially blocked him.

Condo buildings are quietly losing value

In New Orleans, a federal contractor told MarketWatch that the condo unit he paid $90,000 for in 2005 would fetch at most $110,000 two decades on if he were to sell, by his estimate.

Not only is the building within a flood zone, but many residents weren't paying their HOA fees, leaving the HOA underfunded and potentially unable to pay for structural repairs if there were an emergency.

"No amount of cajoling or liens will scare" the owners who don't pay, the former U.S. Marine, who wanted to remain anonymous, told MarketWatch. He pays about $400 a month in HOA fees and plans to move next year, but he is aware that selling will be a pain. He is hoping for a cash sale so that he can at least pay off the remaining $25,000 balance on his mortgage.

"It could take months or years to find a buyer," the veteran added, because the lack of insurance is going to be a big issue.

Would he buy in a condominium again? "Hell no," he said.

(MORE TO FOLLOW) Dow Jones Newswires

data.title: 90% of retirees are making this miscalculation with their savings
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

The order in which you spend your money makes a difference for your taxes - and your enjoyment of life

Saving your IRA to spend last might not be the best financial decision.

When you retire, you ideally have a couple different buckets of money to draw from - like pretax, Roth, cash and Social Security - which helps you diversify your income sources and better manage your taxes.

But retirees are marking their IRAs and 401(k)s as off-limits for a decade or more, and then only taking from them sparingly, according to a new report from Vanguard, one of the biggest retirement-account custodians. This leads to people constraining their budgets early in retirement, and dying with even more money than they started with at the beginning of retirement.

It's a reactive strategy to calm the fear of running out of money, and it ends up working far better than they expect - which is actually counter to their intentions.

"In the savings phase, we do so much to help people auto-enroll, auto-invest - and when it comes to retirement income, we drop them in the Pacific Ocean and say, 'swim,'" said Fiona Greig, Vanguard's global head of investor research and policy. "Maybe it's no surprise to see people struggling."

Vanguard first saw this behavior in blind administrative data from the millions of accounts it manages. It could see that most people waited until they hit the age of required minimum distributions (RMDs) - 73 now, though it will be 75 for those born 1960 and later - and then they tended to only take out the required amount. That RMD is pegged to a government formula based on a person's projected lifespan, and it starts out at about 4% of the account value but is larger at older ages. Following that path of withdrawals and average account growth of 7%, a person would have a greater balance at the end than when they started.

"The end" in this scenario is literal - it's the end of the saver's lifetime. Then the question becomes: What's the point of retirement savings if you have more when you die than when you started retirement, and meanwhile you're living on peanut butter and jelly?

Greig said this is when her team decided to delve deeper, because just looking at back-end data didn't let them see if this was a true behavioral phenomenon, or if it was just a data artifact because Vanguard doesn't necessarily hold each participant's entire life savings. People regularly have accounts at several different institutions at the same time.

So Vanguard surveyed retirees across the income spectrum about how they spent through their entire retirement nest eggs. The results were shockingly the same: Only 1 in 10 retirees took consistent withdrawals from their accounts throughout retirement. Most took sporadic lump sums at times when they had large expenses, or they took one annual distribution once they hit RMD age - and took only the amount required.

The risk of this, Vanguard said, is that this strategy means "backloading income into later years," which can increase income taxes and lead to higher taxes on Social Security and possible monthly surcharges on Medicare, known as IRMAA. It also led to excess money at the end of life - a stated goal of only 1% of the respondents.

"As researchers, we think about smoothing consumption," said Greig. "But using the RMD amount as the retirement income strategy effectively means they go from earning to living on PB&J and just Social Security to having to take out substantial withdrawals, with substantial tax impact, when RMDs kick in."

Spend now or later?

With the data, Vanguard mapped out four different scenarios for a "typical" retiree, with the example of somebody who had $360,000 when they started retirement.

The most common approach was to wall off the pretax savings in IRAs or 401(k)s - or a combination of pretax accounts - and claim Social Security when they hit 62. That carried them until they hit RMD age at 73 or 75. That gave them about $48,000 in annual spending, and at the end of life (an educated estimate) they'd have $398,000.

The second and third options were for the hypothetical person to take regular monthly withdrawals from the $360,000, akin to a paycheck, or to annuitize 25% of their money. Either approach would free up a few thousand dollars more to spend each year. They'd die with less than they started with, because the paycheck would cost them some of their principal, but they'd still have $160,000 or more remaining.

The fourth option was the optimal smoothing that economists propose. Instead of claiming Social Security and waiting to take money from the pretax account, you'd flip that and take money out from your retirement savings for a "bridge paycheck" that would cover you until you turn 70. Your Social Security benefit would grow and by the time you claim, you'd have $56,000 to spend each year - the highest of all the strategies. It's also potentially much more for you to spend on yourself, rather than pay in taxes or Medicare charges along the way. When you die, you'd be projected to have about $44,000 left - not nothing, but not as much of a legacy.

"You're basically buying an annuity," said Aaron Goodman, a Vanguard researcher who worked on the report. "Purely in terms of returns, it makes a lot of sense, because the increase in Social Security by waiting is a guaranteed 7% to 8%. That's an attractive return."

That said, Goodman said that for people with more limited savings, if they have to spend down principal in order to delay, that might be limiting. "It comes down to a choice for the retiree," he said.

For Greig, the decision would be easy: Spend more now and not try to end up with more than she started with after she's gone.

"But that's really a question for each human being," she added. "We see people struggling to spend down their assets, and this is an area where we think more work needs to be done in terms of policy and plan design. We have to make retirement income easy, and the data is showing it's hard for people to do this."

Got a question about retirement? Fill out our new questionnaire or write to me directly at beth.pinsker@marketwatch.com (please put "Fix My Portfolio" in the subject line).

You can also join the Retirement conversation in our Facebook community: Retire Better with MarketWatch.

By submitting your story to Dow Jones & Co., the publisher of MarketWatch, you understand and agree that we may use your story, or versions of it, in all media and platforms, including via third parties.

data.title: Insta360 Opens First Flagship Store Outside Asia In New York's Times Square Amid Global Retail Expansion

Insta360 Opens First Flagship Store Outside Asia In New York's Times Square Amid Global Retail Expansion

Insta360 Opens First Flagship Store Outside Asia In New York's Times Square Amid Global Retail Expansion

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Sept. 19, 2026

NEW YORK, Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Insta360 officially opened its first flagship retail store outside of Asia on Saturday, September 19, 2026, occupying a prime location at 1515 Broadway in New York's Times Square. The store opening marks a major milestone in the global imaging brand's international expansion, underscoring its maturity, scale, and long-term commitment to supporting the U.S. market.

The New York flagship arrives as Insta360 surpasses 10 million cameras shipped worldwide, signaling a new stage of global brand momentum and strong leadership in the camera market. According to IDC, Insta360 ranked No.1 in the global 360° camera market, maintaining a significant lead over competitors with a shipment share of nearly 70% in Q1 this year.

The launch is also part of a broader physical retail strategy that includes a flagship store opened in Tokyo in August, dozens of authorized stores across Asia, and planned European expansion into cities such as Munich.

Establishing a Permanent Footprint in a Priority Market
Insta360 has cultivated strong momentum in the United States since entering the market in 2016, establishing clear category leadership in 360º Cameras*†. Opening an owned flagship in Times Square demonstrates confidence in future North American growth and a desire to build deeper, lasting connections within the U.S. creator ecosystem.

"Reaching 10 million cameras shipped worldwide is a milestone we owe to our community, but opening in Times Square is about building lasting roots," said Max Richter, Co-founder and VP of Marketing at Insta360. "This store opening is about more than just selling into the U.S.; it reflects our long-term commitment to the American creator ecosystem. We look forward to continuing our support for local creators, connecting directly with everyday users, and making innovative imaging tech approachable for anyone with a story to tell."

Democratizing Creativity from Online Awareness to Offline Experience
While Insta360 originally built global awareness through viral social media content and digital channels, the Times Square flagship introduces a permanent physical touchpoint designed to make creative technology accessible to everyone. The store serves as an experience center, offering hands-on product trials, in-person education, technical support, and community space.

By letting visitors test 360, action, gimbal, and wearable cameras in person, the store bridges the gap between online visibility and real-world understanding—helping consumers move from recognizing viral videos to learning how the technology works and capturing their own everyday moments.

"We are thrilled to welcome an innovative, industry-leading brand like Insta360 to the Crossroads of the World," said Tom Harris, President of the Times Square Alliance. "Times Square has always been a global stage for creativity, culture, and cutting-edge technology, making it the perfect home for Insta360's flagship store and a fantastic addition to our dynamic retail landscape."

Grand Opening Highlights
The grand opening at 1515 Broadway featured a day of immersive brand experiences and celebration dedicated to Insta360's growing New York City community. Insta360 Co-founder and VP of Marketing Max Richter led the official ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside renowned filmmaker Casey Neistat. A longtime user of Insta360 technology, Neistat's participation underscores the brand's deep-rooted connection to the professional creator community. The event also featured YouTubers Jesse Wellens and Jeana Smith—both veteran advocates of the brand—who served as honorary store managers, providing hands-on product walkthroughs and engaging directly with local users.

In a nod to Insta360's action-first spirit, the brand also hosted a "Ride Bold" rally, a cycling event that sent 100 riders past iconic New York landmarks to capture the city using Insta360 hardware. The opening attracted long lines of customers waiting outside the store for hours for a chance to explore interactive camera demos, enjoy exclusive opening-day giveaways, and interact with honorary store managers.

*Source: Circana, LLC, Retail Tracking Service, US, Camcorders by Brand, 360 Degrees Capable, Dollar & Unit Sales, Jan 2020 - Feb 2025 Combined
†360° Camera is defined by Circana as camcorders with video and 360-degree view capability.

About Insta360
With a "Think bold" mindset, Insta360 empowers people to capture and share their lives in extraordinary ways. Recognized as a market leader and innovator, Insta360's vast lineup includes the world's best-selling 360 cameras in the X Series, the thumb-sized GO Series for everyday capture, as well as an extensive range of action cameras, gimbals, webcams, and professional photography solutions. With intuitive, AI-powered software, Insta360 simplifies the creative process, allowing users to focus on storytelling without technical barriers. Insta360 is dedicated to helping a new generation of athletes, creatives, travelers and professionals bring their ideas to life.

data.title: Many young investors can't afford to invest without their parents' help
data.description:
By Venessa Wong

Parents are providing help with things like housing and groceries, and sometimes directly investing for their children, to give them a head start in a challenging economy

Help with everyday expenses such as groceries and gas can give young adults the financial breathing room to start investing sooner, according to a new report.

Read more about how young adults are coping with today's economy in MarketWatch's coverage of the New American Playbook.

An affordability crisis is straining American families, but that's not stopping many members of Gen Z from investing in the stock market at younger ages - often with some form of support from their parents, who are making sacrifices to help them get ahead.

In many cases, this doesn't mean a direct investment into a child's account.

"For many younger investors, help with everyday expenses creates financial breathing room that can make regular market contributions possible," according to a new survey of investors ages 18 to 34 and parents of young adults conducted by MarketWise, an investment research company.

Among surveyed parents, 57% said they were helping their adult children pay for groceries, while 56% paid their phone bill, 45% provided funds for housing or let their children live at home for free, and 22% were making car payments for their adult children.

These expenses can add up to hundreds or even thousands of dollars each month. The findings come as young people may see stock-market returns as providing a surer path to wealth than paychecks from a 9-to-5 job.

As young Americans struggle with housing affordability - with the typical rent at $1,948 in August, according to Zillow - 25% of young investors who are living rent-free with their parents said they would own no investments at all without their help, and half said their monthly investing would stop if they didn't receive support.

"Depending on where you live," even an income of $100,000 "can be just barely enough or nowhere near it," Audrey Emerson, the owner of Cents of Joy Financial Planning in Bellingham, Wash., recently told MarketWatch. This is especially true for young adults with children.

Related: More 20-somethings are moving in with their parents. Here's how they can build savings - without bankrupting mom and dad

"Family help often acts more like a runway than an engine. It makes it easier to get off the ground, but the young investor is still making decisions and putting in their own money over time," Steven Longenecker, senior editor at MarketWise, told MarketWatch regarding his company's survey.

At a time when Americans' grasp of personal-finance concepts is on the decline and many students don't receive training in financial literacy in school, providing support "doesn't require writing a check," he added. "A parent who helps a child understand a 401(k), opens the conversation about investing, or encourages them to put away even $20 or $50 regularly can give them a starting point into investing that won't jeopardize the parent's own finances."

Meanwhile, 35% of the surveyed young investors - defined as those holding at least one investment account, including any retirement accounts - said they received money from their family that they invested, while16% received a deposit directly into a brokerage account and 13% received a deposit into a retirement account.

Two-thirds of parents told MarketWise that providing this support was hurting them financially, including by reducing the amount they are able to save for themselves (43%), reducing or delaying travel (24%), and adding to debt (24%).

"It's not surprising that young adults are leaning on both family and nontraditional sources for support, but these dynamics are also putting pressure on parents," Emily Irwin, head of private wealth planning at Wells Fargo, said in a statement earlier this year.

In Wells Fargo's survey, two-thirds of parents of adult Gen Z-ers - the generation born between 1997 and 2012 - said they provide financial support to their children. "Open communication, clear expectations, and shared planning can help families navigate this stage together," Irwin said.

More on this: The kids are out of the house, and I saved for college. How are they still spending so much of my money?

"If a parent has the means to help, I think being explicit about the purpose of the money can be valuable, like explaining that you're helping them now because starting early gives their money more time to compound," Longenecker said.

Young investors' most common holdings were mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (71%), followed by individual tech stocks (32%) and other individual stocks (38%), while 30% owned cryptocurrencies, according to MarketWise.

data.title: The future of retirement? Work until you die.
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

Social Security, once seen as 'old-age insurance,' will eventually disappear, this author predicts

About 19% of Americans age 65 and older participated in the labor force in 2025, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The retirement myth of endless golf games or fishing trips melting into decades of elder bliss has been crumbling for decades.

The idea of retirement as a period of contented leisure has come and gone, said Lawrence Samuel, cultural historian and author of the new book "The Rise and Fall of Retirement in the United States: A Social History." He believes the modern era of retirement is over, and even expects Social Security to eventually "go away" amid a new model in which people work longer into their old age.

"It's a very powerful myth. It's almost like the American dream - it's a myth. But a lot of people think it's an entitlement: 'Where's my American dream?' But most Americans don't realize their American dream. The odds are against you," Samuel told MarketWatch.

The notion of retirement itself is a modern concept, Samuel argued - one showing up in the 20th century and propped up by industries such as travel and housing that created retirement communities, financial institutions that oversaw savings and investing, as well as marketing machines that had consumer products to sell. Before then, people often worked until they died.

"Retirement just came along and became this monolithic concept," Samuel said.

"The myth is still around. Some people still believe it. The classic narrative can be very fulfilling for some people," Samuel added. "Over the decades, the cracks in the narrative began as early as in the 1950s, when retirement was in full bloom. You started seeing evidence that it wasn't a perfect model."

Many older Americans struggle with lack of purpose or structure, as well as loneliness and isolation. The average retiree watches 47 hours of television a week, according to consultancy AgeWave. Loneliness is so bad that in 2023 the U.S. Surgeon General called it an epidemic as deadly as smoking smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day. It's also linked with a greater risk of cardiovascular disease, dementia, stroke, depression, anxiety and premature death.

Then there's the financial aspect of retirement. As pensions became scarce, Americans were forced to save for their own retirements - and many faltered.

The median amount American workers have saved for retirement is just $955. That figure includes people with no retirement savings at all. Using workers who had at least a positive retirement-savings balance, the median savings totaled $40,000, according to the National Institute of Retirement Security. Americans think they will need to save $1.2 million to retire comfortably, according to Schroders, an asset-management firm.

The future of Social Security? No Social Security.

Meanwhile, Social Security faces insolvency in 2032, at which point beneficiaries will see a 22% cut in benefits unless Congress acts first to shore up the system. Among Americans ages 65 and older, 40% rely on Social Security for half or more of their income, while about 14% of recipients 65 and older depend on it for 90% or more of their income, according to AARP.

Samuel expects Social Security, which provides retirement benefits to more than 68 million older adults, to eventually fade away.

"I think ultimately it will go away; politicians just don't want to go there. It's from the 1930s, from the Depression, and it was catered to the 'Greatest Generation' and it was seen as old-age insurance," Samuel said. "Eventually, we'll move away from that. It could be decades, it could be generations. I don't think it fits in this model of this new thing we're creating of the gig economy and older workers back in the workplace."

When Social Security was created in the 1930s, life expectancy at birth was lower than the retirement age of 65 - roughly 60 years for men and 64 years for women. That life expectancy, however, was heavily skewed by high infant mortality, according to the Social Security Administration.

Now, overall life expectancy in the U.S. is at an average age of 79, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That means people have greater potential for living longer in retirement, running out of money and struggling with purpose in life.

"There's 'haves' and 'have-nots'; haves, who have savings or their nest egg or pensions or 401(k), are able to pursue structure and engagement and meaning and purpose. For a big part of the population, it's about survival - it's about putting food on the table and paying the rent. There need to be resources to connect [age-]55-plus employers to the workers who can fill these slots," Samuel said.

He expects older workers to stay in the workforce longer as Americans live longer. About 19% of Americans age 65 and older participated in the labor force in 2025, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

"Retirement - it's not the right word anymore. Purpose is the right word. Human beings need a reason to wake up and get out of bed every morning," Samuel said. "We're worker bees. We're trained in the Protestant work ethic from day one. We're coming around back to the late 19th century, to where it started before this thing came to be - which is a real positive."

So what's next for retirement? It's over, Samuel said.

"Don't quit. Keep your job - keep it despite having an annoying boss or colleagues. Keep the health insurance coming as long as you can," Samuel said. "Keep your job and try to pursue your passions."

-Jessica Hall

data.title: These are the 10 biggest retirement fears - and what you can do about them
data.description:
By Richard Eisenberg

No amount of wealth can erase retirement worries

Pre-retirees and retirees need to identify their fears and then take steps to address them.

When David Luff, a digital health executive in Portsmouth, N.H., retired last October at 67, his biggest retirement fears were whether he and his wife would have enough money, how much their healthcare would cost and how they would navigate long-term care.

"My fears were about things I can control, not things I can't - like the economy and inflation," Luff said.

His fears are very much in line with the new Retirement Fear Index created by retirement coach David Conti. The monthly index uses artificial intelligence to track 10 types of retirement fears Conti identified, such as market volatility and the combination of healthcare and long-term care costs, with each fear weighted by how much of the national conversation he thinks each commands based on media coverage and social media engagement.

Most retirement fears are actionable

No amount of wealth can dispel retirement worries.

"Even if you have $10 million, you still have fears about retirement," said Conti, who worked in Fidelity's wealth-management department for 18 years. "The good news is that about two-thirds of the index's big 10 fears are actionable. So, with good financial planning and retirement coaching for the nonfinancial side, people can do something about them."

The actionable fears can be reduced through things financial planners address, such as risk management, smart investing and insurance protection. The few that are nonactionable are ones Conti calls "psycho-spiritual" and result from things like family issues.

The Retirement Fear Index is a meta-analysis of 28 sources, including findings from retirement researchers at places like the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College and the Employee Benefit Research Institute, as well as retirement-related news like the latest Social Security solvency estimates from the Social Security Administration trustees.

The Retirement Fear Index's rise and recent drop

This index has been rising mostly steadily and is now nearly 22 percentage points above its December 2025 baseline. Earlier this year, the index-level increases were due to things like inflation-inducing tariffs, higher gas prices stemming from the Iran war, and greater market volatility. The index dropped slightly in August due to cooling inflation and an increase in the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index. But it inched up again in its September reading due to heightened fears about market volatility, outliving savings, housing and cognitive decline.

Conti intentionally created a retirement fear index rather than a retirement anxiety index. "Anxiety is something that might happen in the future and fear is more of a present threat," he said on the "Friends Talk Money podcast I co-host.

The 10 biggest retirement fears

The 10 retirement fears tracked by his index, listed from highest weighting to lowest:

-- Healthcare and long-term-care costs

-- Outliving savings/longevity risk

-- Social Security and pension insolvency

-- Inflation and rising everyday costs

-- Cognitive decline/loss of independence

-- Market volatility and sequence-of-returns (the risk that poor investment returns early in retirement would reduce retirees' portfolios)

-- Loss of purpose/identity crisis

-- Housing affordability and maintenance

-- Family caregiving burdens and isolation

-- Taxes and regulatory changes

Several of these top fears aren't financial. "Retirement is really not about money; it's about living life," said Conti.

He thinks it's understandable why healthcare costs and long-term care costs are the No. 1 fear.

"The fear is: 'What if I have a health event or something happens to my spouse?' What are we going to do? Who's going to pay for it?'" Conti said on the podcast. Only about 10% of Americans have long-term-care insurance, he noted. People often overestimate how much Medicare covers those specific needs, such as a nursing home stay or custodial care.

Although taxes and regulatory changes get the lowest weighting in the index, Conti said Americans need to plan more for potential tax expenses in retirement. "In terms of retirement budgeting, it's one of the top categories retirees do not budget for because people don't think much about it," Conti said.

He has his eyes on a few things that could alter the trajectory of the Retirement Fear Index: this fall's announcement of the size of Medicare Part B premiums in 2027, the Social Security trustees' 2027 report, and the 2028 presidential election. Those three events can increase costs in retirement or raise concerns about retirement security.

How to address your retirement fears

The key takeaway from the Retirement Fear Index, said Conti, is that pre-retirees and retirees need to identify their fears and then take steps to address them.

You may not be able to do anything about the fear that Social Security might shrink your benefits due to its solvency challenges. But you can take precautionary steps to lower your expenses and become less dependent on government retirement income. For example, Conti said, "You can reduce your debt."

If you fear healthcare costs in retirement, "start learning about Medicare," Conti advised. Open enrollment season is starting in October, and current and future participants can get an idea of the types of plans available in their areas. This is a good time to review current medical needs, such as medications and doctor visits, as well as assess what type of healthcare will be likely in the coming year, including a procedure or a new prescription.

Concerned about your health worsening in retirement? Exercise more and eat healthier, Conti said.

That's what Luff is doing. "I'm spending more time on my health, probably working out two or three hours a day now," he said. "When you're working, you kind of ignore your health."

If you're nervous about long-term care if you need it, you could do what Luff has done: Look into nearby continuing care residential communities. You move into one of their independent living units and one day, if necessary, you can transfer to one of their assisted living residences.

"If we could get into a place like that, it will be there to take care of us," Luff said.

-Richard Eisenberg

data.title: What happens if you never buy a house? What -2-
data.description:
"That's probably the most important channel through which buying a home builds wealth," said James Choi, a professor of finance at the Yale School of Management, who has challenged traditional personal-finance advice in his research.

The earlier someone becomes a homeowner, the more equity they may be able to accumulate in their home by retirement, assuming about average annual appreciation. They can also end up with significantly lower housing costs at a time when they might have a fixed income. Take a 30-year-old who buys a home for $405,400 - around the median price in the U.S. - using a 30-year mortgage. By the time that person turns 65, they will have nearly $1.6 million in home equity and no monthly mortgage payment, according to a calculator developed by Zandi. But if they wait until age 40 to buy that house - an increasingly common scenario - their housing wealth will be slightly more than $1 million at 65 and they'll still be making mortgage payments. And if they buy at age 45, they'll have $888,281 in equity when they're 65 and will be on the hook for monthly payments for the first 10 years of retirement.

These calculations assume a 6.1% mortgage rate, a 20% down payment and a 4% annual home appreciation rate.

People who are priced out of buying a home can still build wealth without owning one. In many of these scenarios, someone who rents for decades actually comes out ahead, wealthwise, if they're able to invest a relatively significant sum - about $800 a month in the early years of building their portfolio, according to Zandi's calculator. That assumes an 8% annual stock-market return and 3% annual rent increases.

"It's not clear that there's this huge financial advantage to owning a home if you are saving outside of the home," Choi said.

Caleb Pepperday is a financial planner who works with clients who are largely between 30 and 50 years old and are physician assistants. Many of them own homes, but he says the ones that don't aren't necessarily rushing to buy. In some cases, they're seeing that home prices and interest rates are so high that investing in a house doesn't feel worth it right now. In the meantime, these clients are saving in buckets outside of retirement accounts to give themselves the option to use that money to buy a home at some point - or simply to continue to build wealth.

Caleb Pepperday has experience as a homeowner - but for now, he's renting.

Pepperday has personal experience with both arrangements. He and his wife owned a home in Pittsburgh and lived there for two years, then sold it when his wife, who works as a physician assistant, was offered a job in Montana. For now, they're renting.

"We don't know how long we're going to stay here, so we didn't want to lock up money in a house," he said.

For clients who are renting, Pepperday looks for ways to help them put their money to work besides investing in a house.

"We've seen parents or grandparents use homes as the way to build wealth," he said. "Now there's alternatives that potentially weren't around back when my parents and my grandparents were around. People are starting to understand that buying a house isn't the only way to build wealth."

Americans have easier access to investments outside of housing than previous generations did, Zandi said - pointing to the popularization of index funds launched in the 1970s and automatic 401(k) contributions. "The stock market is just a much bigger market, just a much more liquid market" than it used to be, he noted.

But an investor who is relying on the stock market to build wealth needs the psychological fortitude to keep putting money into the market, even during a downturn, he added. "Investing in housing is much more straightforward," Zandi said.

Some younger homeowners and renters challenge the idea that a home should be their primary asset.

Jesse Beeler first became a homeowner when he was 23 years old, and since then, he has sold that house and bought another one. Still, Beeler - who lives in Greencastle, a small city in the south-central part of Pennsylvania - said he might have chosen to rent if he lived in a different location with a more robust rental market, and if he hadn't internalized the financial advice of his parents' generation when he was in his early 20s.

"I don't know if the rewards of owning a home match the risk profile of today's economy," said Beeler, who is now 30. "It's kind of an investment that you can't really get to without either borrowing against it or selling, which then upends your life. For me, it just doesn't feel like it's liquid enough."

For Jesse Beeler and his wife, there are benefits to homeownership, including the opportunity to increase the value of their home by renovating the kitchen and doing other projects. But he's skeptical owning a home can be a reliable source of wealth.

Given today's relatively high interest rates, Beeler, who works in supply-chain finance, said he feels like he's paying a premium to the bank to own his home, although he recognizes there are benefits to owning. He and his wife, who is a teacher, were able to buy a place that's close to family and to the school where she works. They also have the opportunity to increase the value of their home by renovating the kitchen and doing other projects.

Nonetheless, he's skeptical that owning a home can be a reliable source of wealth, and when he looks at retirement projections, he doesn't factor in his home. The idea - prominent among his parents' generation - that you need to own a home to achieve financial independence is "pretty flawed," he said. "It was passed heavily on to me."

Still want to buy a home? It might get easier.

For many, though, the desire to own a home isn't all about building the biggest nest egg. Instead, it's about stability, being part of a community or getting access to a particular type of housing.

"The types of things that are available to buy are different from the types of homes that are available to rent," said Choi. Though developers are building more single-family homes specifically as rentals, that kind of housing stock is typically more readily available to buyers. And if you want to be able to make changes to your living space over time and you plan to stay in the same location long term, buying can make sense.

The tax code provides some advantages to homeowners, and a mortgage allows buyers to own a large asset with a relatively small initial investment. Though the total annual cost of homeownership has become more difficult for buyers to predict in recent years, given rising insurance premiums and property taxes, owning a home with a fixed-rate mortgage can help stabilize your housing costs.

And in a period of high inflation, like the one we're living through now, a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage can act as an inflation hedge. As prices broadly go up, your payment can, over time, feel like less of a burden. For example, the median mortgage payment for homeowners who moved in 2024 and 2025 was $2,300, according to the Federal Reserve. After 10 years, that $2,300 will feel like about $1,700 today, assuming a 3% rate of inflation.

And although we're living through a historically challenging period to purchase a home, the good news is that there are signs it may get easier. Because prices are so high right now, there's little room for them to keep growing, according to Zandi.

"You could get affordability restored not because you have more supply, but less demand," he said, noting that it's "almost a demographic certainty as you move into the 2030s." The drop in U.S. immigration is likely to dampen demand for homes, according to Zandi, while the declining birth rate, coupled with aging baby boomers who will be letting go of their homes in the coming years, could also play a role in decreasing demand.

For years, Zandi has been saying some version of the line that, for most people, renting makes more sense than buying a home. But as the years go by and the demographic realities start to change, he thinks he may be saying that with less and less confidence, until it's no longer true.

In Los Angeles, Saunders says it's hard to imagine that future, at least for now. When she looks around at her peers, most are renting or living with their parents. Many, like her, are struggling to keep up with the expenses of daily living, let alone setting aside enough money to invest in an asset like a home.

Sometimes, Saunders wonders whether the path she followed - go to college, get a job - would have led to her owning a home if she'd come of age in a different generation.

"I had to quell those desires for homeownership as I continue to see the price of everything grow exponentially," she said.
